title: What Young learned: timing, building a solo, stage presentation
summary: From Armstrong he learned to build slowly, relax on stage and read an audience.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Do you know of any specific ways of the playing or the singing you changed from having been associated with Louis? What were --

I don't know. I would say I learned a lot about timing from Louis. I learned a lot about building, like not starting out too strong, just building things and, you know, starting easy and building things up. And these things are important.

But timing, I think the greatest thing I accomplished from Louis was not trying to put everything into -- right away into something, not trying to do all the things I knew right away into a chorus, but taking it easy and building the thing up to a climax, you know. And he was a master at that. But
some guys you hear, they start out like a house a-fire. Then they kind of calm down. But that wasn't his way of doing things. He started out easy, and he would build. He had a climax going.

I learned that from him. I -- I certainly learned stage presentation from him, because I learned how to handle myself on the stage, you know, for -- to relax more on the stage, not get out there and jump up and down like a bouncing ball or something and beat my brains out. You know, some guys go --
No, but I learned not to do it, to be much more relaxed; like some people, when they get out there, they're jumping up and down so much, they can't hold their horn straight and play right, you know.

He was relaxed, and this guy was -- he had the whole thing, really. Believe me, he had the whole thing going there. He was -- he was complete. And he knew the stage;like, for instance, we'd start playing a thing some nights, and he wouldn't -- he wouldn't like the way the

way the response was, and right away he'd change and go into something. He wouldn't do the regular thing, you know. He'd go into something else. He'd handle them, you know. He knew how to -- he knew people. He could -- he could read an audience. And this is hard to do. It's very hard to do.

I've seen some top musicians that -- Benny couldn't do it. I've seen some very fine, excellent musicians that couldn't read that audience. They would -- they would give the wrong program. It was good, but they played -- you could find no fault with it. It would be flawless almost, but it would be the wrong presentation for that particular audience.

This is what he knew. Nobody could teach you that. These are things you try to watch and pick out, and I guess it took him years to become, to get to that point where he could really do that. But I watched him. I watched him like a hawk.
